meta.title: "I feel it, so it must be true" — why your child gets confused when opinions are passed off as facts | Sila Slova
meta.description: Teach your child to tell facts from opinions and stop taking other people's feelings as proof. Game-based course for children aged 8–12.

hero.headline: "I feel it, so it must be true!" — and your child is already doubting themselves?
hero.subheadline: An opinion is being presented as a fact. It sounds convincing — but there's nothing to check. This isn't proof. It's a substitution.

media.alt: A child confused between a fact and an opinion presented as truth

pain.title: A feeling isn't a fact. But that's exactly how it gets presented
pain.body:
"I feel like that's wrong", "it seems to me like it's your fault", "it's definitely true because I think so". At school, in arguments, among friends. The child gets confused — it sounds convincing, but they don't know how to check it or whether they even should.

This isn't proof — it's a substitution: a personal feeling is passed off as truth. A fact can be checked — an opinion is just someone's judgement. When the two get mixed up, it seems pointless to argue because "that's just how the person feels". Without the skill to tell them apart, the child starts to doubt themselves.

The result — they agree with something that has no real evidence behind it. Simply because someone sounded confident.

solution.title: "Sila Slova" — a detective drama that teaches critical thinking
solution.body: 40 episodes, 13 critical thinking lessons. Your child plays — but is actually learning to protect themselves.
bullets: 🔍 Tells facts apart from opinions and personal feelings
🧠 Asks "can this be checked?" — and waits for a real answer
💬 Doesn't automatically accept other people's feelings as truth
🛡️ Doesn't doubt themselves when someone speaks confidently but without evidence

social_proof.quote: Now when a classmate says "I feel like you're wrong", my daughter asks: "Is there any proof of that?" Short, calm, no conflict. I couldn't do that at her age.
social_proof.author: Valentyna, mum of 11-year-old Polina

faq.q: Is it a game or a learning course?

faq.q: What age is it suitable for?
